questions.question: Distinguish between superimposed and antecedent drainage, stating the age relationship that defines each and the shared landform evidence.
questions.expected_answer: In superimposed drainage the buried structure is older: the river develops its course on a young cover of rock and, as it erodes downward, is let down onto the older folded structure beneath, keeping its inherited course and cutting gorges across ridges. In antecedent drainage the river is older: it existed before folding or uplift raised land across its path, and its downcutting kept pace with the rising structure. Both produce the same evidence — a river crossing high ground through a deep gorge instead of flowing around it.

questions.question: Describe the process of eutrophication in the correct sequence, naming the nutrient sources and a South African example.
questions.expected_answer: Nutrients — nitrates and phosphates from fertilised farmland, failing sewage works and detergents — enrich the water; algae bloom explosively; the bloom blocks sunlight so submerged plants die; the algae then die, and bacterial decomposition of the dead material consumes the dissolved oxygen; the oxygen crashes and fish and other aquatic life suffocate, leaving a green, near-lifeless water body. Hartbeespoort Dam, with its pea-green blooms and hyacinth mats, is the standing South African example.

questions.question: Present the Working for Water programme as a South African catchment management case study: name, date, problem, method and results.
questions.expected_answer: Working for Water is a national programme running since 1995. The problem: invasive alien plants — wattle, gum, pine and hakea — infest catchments and riverbanks, consuming far more water than indigenous vegetation, displacing fynbos and intensifying wildfires. The method: labour-intensive clearing by cutting, herbicide and burning, catchment by catchment, with follow-up to prevent regrowth. The results are a double dividend: measured streamflow returned to rivers and dams, and employment and training for tens of thousands of people from poor rural communities, including women-led teams — a world-first model that requires permanent follow-up to remain effective.
